title: Reading a Drawing Like an Inspector: What I Check First
excerpt: A drawing says more than dimensions. Here is the quick pass I make before a part ever touches a gauge — five minutes that save an afternoon.
content:
A part is only wrong relative to something. Before I pick up a caliper, I want to know exactly what that something is. This is the pass I make on every new drawing — five minutes that save an afternoon.

## 1. Title block and revision
The first question is never "what is this dimension?" It is "am I looking at the current revision?" Check the drawing number, revision letter, part name, material and the notes block. On the shop floor, an old print is a quality escape waiting to be measured.

## 2. The datum scheme
Look at the datum features before the dimensions. Datums tell you how the part is supposed to sit in space. A dimension measured from the wrong datum is not a measurement — it is an opinion. On pressings and castings, the datum choice often decides whether the part passes or fails.

## 3. Critical characteristics
Scan for tight tolerances, GD&T frames, surface finish callouts and notes like "no tool marks". These are the features I plan instruments for first. A profile projector, surface tester or CMM may be needed where a caliper is not enough.

## 4. Material, finish and process notes
Material and process notes change the measurement strategy. An aluminium casting expands differently from a steel forging. A welded assembly needs to be checked after cooling, not immediately after the torch stops. Heat treatment, plating and coating notes matter too — a plated part may need to be measured before the coating.

## 5. QSR / CMR status
If the part is a QSR or CMR part, the stakes are higher: documentation, traceability and approval discipline come before convenience. I check what records are required before the part moves, not after.

## 6. Mating interfaces
I ask which features touch other parts. The closest tolerances usually belong to mating faces and bores, not to the features that are easiest to measure. Knowing the interface helps me explain why a deviation matters — or why it does not.

## 7. The measurement plan
Finally, I decide how to measure before touching the part: instruments, fixtures, number of checks, and what "repeatable" looks like. If I measure the same feature twice and get two different stories, I stop.

> A measurement you cannot repeat is just a number.

None of this is glamorous. But most inspection disputes I have seen were not about a hard measurement — they were about a drawing that was read too quickly. Slow down at the start, and the gauge becomes a formality.

title: GOM Alignment Explained: Local Best Fit, PLP and RPS
excerpt: The same scan can pass or fail depending on alignment. A practical look at choosing between Local Best Fit, PLP and RPS — and why the method belongs in the report.
content:
A scan is a cloud of points. An inspection is a decision. Between the two sits the alignment — the step that tells the software where your part sits relative to the CAD model. The same physical part can look good or bad depending on how you align it, so the method has to match the question.

## What GOM is actually doing
The process is straightforward: scan the part, turn the scan into a mesh or point cloud, align it to the CAD, then compare surface deviation and features. GOM shows you colour maps and numbers. The alignment step decides which numbers you get.

## Local Best Fit
Local Best Fit aligns a selected region of the part to the CAD, optimising the fit in that area. It is useful when the question is about the form or profile of a specific feature — a sealing face, a rib, a local surface. The trade-off: a local fit can hide a global shift. If the whole part has moved, a local alignment can still show a neat, green colour map in the region you selected.

Use it when the question is local, and say so in the report.

## PLP
PLP is an alignment built from basic geometry — a point, a line and a plane — the classic way of fixing the six degrees of freedom. It follows the drawing's datum logic closely, which makes it a strong choice when the drawing defines primary, secondary and tertiary datums. It is less forgiving than a best fit, and that is often the point.

## RPS
RPS (Reference Point System) aligns the part through reference points. In automotive work this usually reflects how the part is located in its fixture or in the vehicle. It answers a functional question: how does this part sit when it is actually used?

That makes RPS my default when a customer asks whether a casting or pressing will assemble correctly.

## Choosing between them
I ask three questions:

- Is the question about a local feature or the whole part?
- Which datum scheme does the drawing define?
- How is the part located in real life?

Functional position means RPS. Drawing datums mean PLP. A local feature means Local Best Fit. When in doubt, run more than one and label each result.

## What I put in the report
The alignment screenshot, the method used, the reference features, and the software version. A deviation number without the alignment method is incomplete information. On the Bajaj Auto program, this discipline was as important as the scan quality itself. Castings, weldments and pressings each behaved differently, and the conversation went much faster when everyone knew which alignment produced the number.

Terminology and best practice vary between companies and customers. Always follow the approved quality plan first; treat this as a way to ask better questions, not a replacement for it.

title: From Diploma to Shop Floor: My First Year as a Jr. Engineer
excerpt: I had CATIA and AutoCAD on my CV. What I did not have was shop-floor judgement. Six lessons from my first year at Bajaj Auto's Chakan plant.
content:
I finished my diploma in Mechanical Engineering at Puranmal Lahoti Government Polytechnic, Latur, in October 2020. In December 2021 I joined Accurate Engineering as a Jr. Engineer and was deployed to the Bajaj Auto plant at Chakan. I had CATIA and AutoCAD on my CV. What I did not have was shop-floor judgement.

Here is what the first year actually taught me.

## 1. The drawing is the contract
College projects let you interpret. A production drawing does not. I learned to check the revision, the datum scheme and the notes before measuring anything. Most of my early mistakes were not measurement mistakes — they were reading mistakes.

## 2. Instruments have habits
A profile projector, a surface tester, a caliper, a gauge — each has its own setup, care and repeatability. I kept a small notebook of quirks: how a particular fixture seats, where a zero drifts, which surface needs a wipe first. That notebook was more useful than any manual.

## 3. Ask why the deviation matters
My first instinct was to report a number. The useful instinct is to understand the consequence. Does this face mate with something? Is the bore a locating feature? Is this a QSR or CMR part? When I could explain the "so what", the conversation with production changed completely.

## 4. Measure twice, especially when you are sure
Sample parts, machined and forged, taught me that repeatability is the quiet foundation of quality. If two measurements of the same feature disagree, the part is not the only thing that needs investigation.

## 5. Documentation is part of the job
Handling QSR and CMR parts, calibration records and inspection reports showed me that a good measurement is only half the work. The other half is proving later that the measurement was made correctly, on the right revision, with a calibrated instrument.

## 6. People are part of the process
Quality is not a department that says no. It is a conversation with production, the customer and the measurement lab. The best inspectors I met were calm, specific and impossible to argue with — because their evidence was clean.

In July 2024 I moved to Sagar Industries, Katraj, as Quality Inspector cum Engineer. The scope changed: daily quality meetings, direct customer handling, and more decisions that have to be made before all the information is available.

If you are a diploma student reading this, my advice is simple. Learn the software, but spend time in the inspection bay. Ask to see a drawing being argued about. That is where the engineering actually happens.

title: Calibration Is the Cheapest Insurance in Manufacturing
excerpt: A gauge is a measuring system, not a fact. Why calibration registers, due-date labels and a little paranoia protect every number you sign.
content:
Two hundredths of a millimetre is nothing. It is thinner than a human hair. On a critical bore, it is also the difference between a shipping part and a scrap part.

That is why I take calibration personally.

## A gauge is a measuring system
A caliper, a micrometer, a profile projector, a surface tester — none of them is "correct" on its own. Each is a system with wear, temperature sensitivity, handling habits and drift. Calibration is how we find out whether the system is still telling the truth.

## What calibration actually says
A calibration certificate does not say "this gauge is perfect". It says the gauge's readings were traceable to a standard, within stated conditions, at a particular time. That distinction matters. A calibrated gauge can still be used badly.

## Habits that make calibration count

- Keep a register: every gauge, its ID, location, calibration date and next due date.
- Label instruments clearly. If the label is missing, the gauge is out of service until it is found.
- Store gauges properly. A caliper thrown into a toolbox is a measurement waiting to become a rumour.
- Check what can be checked before use — zero, cleanliness, battery, damage.
- Never use an overdue gauge for a "quick check". Quick checks are where escapes begin.

## The cost argument
Calibration costs money. Scrap, rework, line stoppage and a customer complaint cost more. In my experience, quality documentation is the cheapest insurance a manufacturing unit can buy — and calibration sits at the top of that list.

## What it looks like on the floor
Part of my work has been hands-on calibration of gauges, along with using profile projectors and surface testers. It changed how I treat every instrument. When I pick up a gauge now, I am not just asking what it reads. I am asking whether I can defend that reading a month from now.

If you do not trust the tool, you cannot trust the number. And if you cannot trust the number, the report is only decoration.

title: QSR and CMR Parts: The Labels That Raise the Standard of Proof
excerpt: Some parts carry an extra label that changes the rules around them. What elevated controls look like in daily inspection work — without pretending one acronym covers every customer.
content:
Every drawing defines a part. Some parts carry an extra label that changes the rules around them. QSR and CMR parts are two of those labels — and learning how to handle them changed the way I think about documentation.

## What the labels mean in practice
The exact definition depends on the customer's quality agreement, so I will not pretend one acronym covers every case. In practice, QSR and CMR parts are subject to elevated controls:

- Stricter inspection and documentation requirements
- Clear traceability from material to shipment
- Measured evidence against drawing and, where relevant, CAD
- Controlled storage and segregation
- Formal approval before the part moves to the next stage
- Re-qualification triggers after process changes

The part itself may be perfectly ordinary. The label is about the consequence of getting it wrong.

## Why they matter
A QSR or CMR tag usually reflects a safety, regulatory or customer-mandated requirement. That means a missing measurement is not a paperwork inconvenience; it is a broken traceability chain. When an auditor or customer asks "how do you know this part is correct?", the answer has to be in the records.

## What I check first

- Is the drawing revision correct?
- Is this part actually on the QSR/CMR list for this program?
- What does the control plan require — features, frequency, instruments?
- Are the gauges calibrated and within due date?
- Are the inspection records complete and signed?
- Is the part segregated correctly from normal production?

## The habits that protect you
Keep the part identity and documents together. Do not borrow a record from a similar part. Do not skip a measurement because the previous batch passed. Escalate a deviation early — bad news does not improve with age.

## A personal note
Handling QSR/CMR parts on the Bajaj Auto program taught me a kind of discipline that is hard to learn from a textbook. The inspection itself was familiar: drawings, gauges, CAD comparison. What changed was the standard of proof. Every number had to be repeatable, traceable and explainable.

That standard is worth keeping even when the label is not there.
